title: Pronunciation for band 9
summary: After this unit you can place stress correctly in academic word families, use weak forms and connected speech, and use stress, chunking and intonation to carry meaning.

lessons.title: Word stress in academic word families

items.title: Why word stress matters at band 9
body: Pronunciation at band 9 is about being 'effortless to understand' and using the full range of features flexibly. A misplaced word stress is one of the few pronunciation errors that genuinely stops a listener: *eCOnomy* said as *ecoNOmy* can make a fluent speaker momentarily unintelligible.

Spanish has fairly predictable stress, often on the second-last syllable, and nearly full vowels in every syllable. English stress moves within word families, and unstressed vowels usually reduce to the weak vowel schwa /ə/. Getting both right is what makes speech sound effortless.
items.tip: When you learn an academic word, learn its stress pattern at the same time. Mark it in your notes: phoTOgraphy, photoGRAPHic.

items.title: Suffixes that move the stress
body: Many suffixes pull the stress to a fixed position. Learn these rules and you can predict most academic words.
In the IPA, the mark ˈ comes before the stressed syllable, and ˌ before a weaker, secondary stress.
list: **-ity**: stress the syllable just before: *PUBlic* becomes *pubLIcity*
**-ee, -eer, -ese**: stress the suffix itself: *refuGEE*, *trainEE*, *engiNEER*, *JapanESE* (*employee* is often *emPLOYee* in British English)

items.title: Nouns and verbs that look the same
body: Many two-syllable words are stressed on the first syllable as nouns and on the second as verbs. This matters whenever you talk about trends and data, in Part 3 especially.

examples.text: There was an increase in demand. Demand began to increase.
She broke the record. They record every lecture.

items.tip: The stress moves: PHO-to-graph, pho-TO-gra-phy, pho-to-GRAPH-ic. Notice how the first vowel weakens to /ə/ in photography.
e-CON-o-my and e-CON-o-mist share a stress; e-co-NOM-ic follows the -ic rule.
AN-a-lyse, a-NAL-y-sis, an-a-LYT-i-cal. The first vowel is full /æ/ only when stressed.
POL-i-tics, po-LIT-i-cal, pol-i-TI-cian. In political the first vowel reduces to /ə/.
The -ity and -ical suffixes pull the stress onto the syllable just before them.

items.text: There was a sharp increase in prices, so the council decided to increase the fees.
items.ipa: /ðə wəz ə ˈʃɑːp ˈɪŋkriːs ɪn ˈpraɪsɪz | səʊ ðə ˈkaʊnsl dɪˈsaɪdɪd tʊ ɪnˈkriːs ðə ˈfiːz/
items.tip: Noun INcrease, verb inCREASE in the same sentence.

items.q: Where is the main stress in *democratic*?
items.why: Words ending in -ic are stressed on the syllable before: /ˌdeməˈkrætɪk/. Compare deMOcracy /dɪˈmɒkrəsi/.

items.q: Which word has a different stress pattern from the others?
items.why: phoTOgraphy, eCOnomy and techNOlogy are all stressed on the second syllable; poliTIcian is stressed on the third, before -ion.

items.q: In 'Exports rose by ten per cent', how is *exports* stressed?
items.why: Here *exports* is a noun (the subject), so it is stressed on the first syllable: /ˈekspɔːts/.

items.q: Choose the stressed syllable in each word.
items.why: a-NAL-y-sis, AN-a-lyse, pub-LIC-i-ty, e-co-NOM-ic, PHO-to-graph, re-fu-GEE (-ee takes the stress).

items.title: Weak forms: the secret of natural rhythm
body: English is stress-timed: stressed syllables come at roughly regular intervals, and the small grammar words in between are squeezed. Words like *a, the, of, to, for, and, can, was, were, have, them* are normally pronounced in their **weak form**, with the vowel reduced to /ə/ or dropped.
Speakers who pronounce every word in full sound careful and slightly robotic, even when every sound is correct. Using weak forms is one of the clearest signs of band 8-9 pronunciation.
list: of: /əv/ or /ə/ (a cup of tea /ə ˈkʌp əv ˈtiː/)
to: /tə/ before consonants (want to go /ˈwɒnt tə ˈɡəʊ/)
items.tip: Grammar words keep their strong form when stressed for contrast or at the end of a sentence: 'Yes, I *can*.' /ˈjes aɪ ˈkæn/.

items.title: Linking, elision and assimilation
body: In connected speech, words run together. Three processes matter most for intelligibility and naturalness.
list: **Linking**: a final consonant joins the next vowel (*an_apple*), and British speakers pronounce a written final r before a vowel, the linking /r/ (*far_away* /ˌfɑːr əˈweɪ/). Many also add an intrusive /r/ where there is no letter r (*the idea_of it* /ðiː aɪˈdɪər əv ɪt/).
**Elision**: /t/ and /d/ between consonants often disappear (*next door* /ˌneks ˈdɔː/, *last night* /ˌlɑːs ˈnaɪt/).
**Assimilation**: sounds change to suit their neighbours (*ten people* /ˌtem ˈpiːpl/, *would you* /ˈwʊdʒu/).

items.text: I was going to ask for a cup of tea.
items.ipa: /aɪ wəz ˈɡəʊɪŋ tʊ ˈɑːsk fər ə ˈkʌp əv ˈtiː/
items.tip: Only four words are stressed: GO-, ASK, CUP, TEA. *Was*, *for*, *a* and *of* are weak. Note the linking /r/ in *for a*.

items.text: There are some of them in the box.
items.ipa: /ðər ə ˈsʌm əv ðəm ɪn ðə ˈbɒks/
items.tip: Listen for how short *there are* becomes: /ðər ə/. *Of them* is /əv ðəm/.

items.text: I can speak French, but I can't write it.
items.ipa: /aɪ kən ˈspiːk ˈfrentʃ | bət aɪ ˈkɑːnt ˈraɪt ɪt/
items.tip: Weak *can* /kən/ versus strong *can't* /kɑːnt/: the vowel difference carries the meaning.

items.text: Yes, I can. And so can she.
items.ipa: /ˈjes aɪ ˈkæn | ən ˈsəʊ kæn ˈʃiː/
items.tip: At the end of a phrase *can* takes its strong form /kæn/. In *so* + auxiliary + subject (*so can she*), *can* also keeps its full vowel /kæn/, although the stresses fall on *so* and *she*.

items.text: We met last night next door to the station.
items.ipa: /wi ˈmet ˌlɑːs ˈnaɪt ˌneks ˈdɔː tə ðə ˈsteɪʃn/
items.tip: Elision: the /t/ disappears in *last night* and *next door*.

items.text: Would you mind if ten people joined us?
items.ipa: /ˈwʊdʒu ˈmaɪnd ɪf ˌtem ˈpiːpl ˈdʒɔɪnd əs/
items.tip: Assimilation: *would you* becomes /ˈwʊdʒu/, and the /n/ in *ten* becomes /m/ before /p/.

items.text: The idea of it is far easier than the reality.
items.ipa: /ðiː aɪˈdɪər əv ɪt ɪz ˌfɑːr ˈiːziə ðən ðə riˈæləti/
items.tip: Intrusive /r/ after *idea* and linking /r/ after *far*: both join a vowel to the next vowel, a key feature of British English.

items.q: In 'I'd like a glass of water', how is *of* normally pronounced?
items.why: Unstressed *of* is /əv/ (or even /ə/ in fast speech). The full form /ɒv/ is used only for emphasis or at the end of a phrase.

items.q: In which sentence is *to* most likely to have a strong form /tuː/?
options: Who did you give it to?
items.why: Prepositions at the end of a sentence take their strong form: *to* /tuː/. Before a verb, *to* is weak /tə/.

Linking and intrusive /r/ join a vowel to a vowel (*law and order* and *media attention* have no written r: intrusive). Elision drops /t/ or /d/ between consonants. Assimilation changes /n/ to /m/ before /b/ or /p/ (*in bed*, *ten boys*).

items.title: Sentence stress carries meaning
body: In a neutral sentence, content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs) are stressed, and the last important word carries the main stress, the **nucleus**. Moving the nucleus changes the meaning, usually to show contrast or correction.
This is a powerful tool in Part 3: stressing the right word lets you contrast ideas without extra words.

examples.text: It's not that people are less *patient*; they're less *used* to waiting.
examples.note: Contrastive stress makes the distinction clear.

items.title: Chunking: speaking in thought groups
body: Fluent speakers divide speech into **thought groups** (tone units), each with one main stress, separated by tiny pauses. Chunking in the right places makes complex sentences easy to follow; pausing in the wrong places (between an article and its noun, for example) makes even simple sentences hard to process.
Chunk boundaries normally fall between clauses and after long subjects or introductory phrases. In IPA transcriptions here, | marks a boundary.

examples.text: The students who had revised | passed easily.
The students, | who had revised, | passed easily.
examples.note: Non-defining: pauses around the extra information. All the students had revised.

items.title: Intonation for meaning and attitude
body: Three tones do most of the work. A **fall** signals completeness or certainty. A **rise** signals a yes/no question or that more is coming. A **fall-rise** signals reservation, contrast or an unfinished thought: *It's a good idea... in theory.*
The fall-rise is especially useful in Part 3 for hedging: it tells the examiner you are qualifying what you say.
list: Fall: *I think it's a positive change.* (certain)
Rise: *Do you mean in cities?* (genuine question)
Fall-rise: *Well, it's cheaper...* (but there's a problem)
Lists: rises on each item, fall on the last: *cost, convenience, and time.*

items.text: I didn't say she stole it; I said she borrowed it.
items.ipa: /aɪ ˈdɪdnt seɪ ʃi ˈstəʊl ɪt | aɪ ˈsed ʃi ˈbɒrəʊd ɪt/
items.tip: Put the main stress on *stole* and *borrowed* to create the contrast.

items.text: It's not that people are less patient; they're just less used to waiting.
items.ipa: /ɪts ˈnɒt ðət ˈpiːpl ə les ˈpeɪʃnt | ðeə dʒəst les ˈjuːst tə ˈweɪtɪŋ/
items.tip: Contrastive stress on *patient* and *used*. A short pause at the semicolon.

items.text: The government, which had promised lower taxes, raised them within a year.
items.ipa: /ðə ˈɡʌvənmənt | wɪtʃ əd ˈprɒmɪst ˈləʊə ˈtæksɪz | ˈreɪzd ðəm wɪðɪn ə ˈjɪə/
items.tip: Three thought groups. The middle one is extra information, said slightly lower and faster.
Use a fall-rise on *cheaper* and *theory* to signal reservation without saying 'but'.

items.text: The main reasons are cost, convenience and time.
items.ipa: /ðə ˈmeɪn ˈriːznz ə ˈkɒst | kənˈviːniəns | ən ˈtaɪm/
items.tip: Rise on *cost* and *convenience*, fall on *time* to show the list is complete.

items.q: 'I didn't buy the *red* car.' What does the speaker imply?
options: Someone else bought the red car.
The speaker rented the red car.
The speaker bought a red bicycle.
The speaker bought a car of a different colour.
items.why: Stress on *red* contrasts the colour: the speaker bought a car, but not the red one.

items.q: Where is the most natural chunk boundary? 'Most of the people I spoke to at the conference were surprisingly optimistic.'
options: Most of the | people I spoke to at the conference were surprisingly optimistic.
Most of the people I spoke to at the conference | were surprisingly optimistic.
Most of the people I spoke | to at the conference were surprisingly optimistic.
Most of the people I spoke to at the | conference were surprisingly optimistic.
items.why: The boundary falls after the long subject, before the verb. The other options split a phrase in the middle.

items.q: A candidate says 'It's a good idea' with a fall-rise on *idea*. What does the examiner hear?
options: Reservation: it's a good idea, but...
items.why: A fall-rise signals an implied 'but', a natural way to hedge in speech.

rows.label: Stating a firm conclusion: 'So, on balance, it's a positive change.'
Hedging: 'It might work... in some cities.'
The last item of a list: '...and transport.'

items.why: Falls signal completion and certainty; rises signal questions and incompleteness; fall-rises signal reservation.
